title: Unit 5: Earth–Sun Relationships — Reasons for the Seasons
sub: Reading: pages 66–75  ·  20 points  ·  15 minutes  ·  Closed book
instructions: Answer every question. For multiple choice, circle the single best answer. Write short answers in complete sentences.

questions.stem: In 1543, who proposed that Earth and the other planets make regular revolutions around the Sun, and that Earth rotates once a day on its axis?
questions.why: p. 67 — a radical idea at the time. It gained acceptance slowly, and our modern view of solar system motion is based on his work.

choices: Earth being physically closer to the Sun in summer
the 23.5° tilt of Earth’s axis combined with Earth’s revolution around the Sun
regular changes in the Sun’s energy output
questions.why: p. 70 — the text names choice (a) explicitly as a common misconception. The tilt means one hemisphere is more directly exposed to the Sun’s rays than the other.

questions.stem: At the Northern Hemisphere’s summer solstice, the Sun’s rays strike Earth most directly along
questions.why: p. 70 — around June 21st or 22nd. At that same moment it is the winter solstice in the Southern Hemisphere.

questions.stem: Which type of ultraviolet radiation does not reach the planet’s surface at all?
questions.why: pp. 68–69 — UVC is the highest energy and is stopped completely. UVB is mostly stopped; UVA, the lowest energy, travels through to the ground. Ozone does most of this filtering.

questions.stem: Compared with one molecule of carbon dioxide, one molecule of methane traps about
questions.why: p. 70 — 10,600 times is CFC-12. Carbon dioxide still matters enormously because it is far more abundant in the atmosphere than either.

choices: the Sun’s rays shine most directly at the equator and daylight and nighttime hours are equal
the North Pole points directly toward the Sun
Earth reaches its closest point to the Sun
the Sun never rises above the horizon at either pole
questions.why: p. 71 — the equinoxes fall halfway between the solstices: the vernal equinox around March 21st or 22nd and the autumnal equinox around September 22nd or 23rd.

questions.stem: About 44% of the solar radiation reaching Earth is in visible light wavelengths.
questions.why: p. 68 — only about 7% is ultraviolet; the remainder is infrared, the longest wavelength, which we feel as heat.

questions.stem: Greenhouse gases are entirely a product of human activity.
questions.why: All of the greenhouse gases listed — CO₂, H₂O, methane, O₃, and nitrous oxides — are a normal part of the atmosphere. CFCs are the single exception. Human activity has, however, sharply raised the levels of several of them. (p. 70)

questions.stem: Explain why the Northern Hemisphere is warmer in June than in December. Your answer should refer both to the directness of the Sun’s rays and to the length of daylight.
questions.answer: In June the North Pole is tilted toward the Sun, so the rays strike more directly and the days are longer; in December the tilt points away, spreading the same light over a larger area for fewer hours.
questions.rubric: 1 pt for the tilt toward/away from the Sun. 1 pt for directness — when the tilt points away, light is spread out over a larger area, so that area is not heated as much. 1 pt for duration — fewer daylight hours in winter means less time for the Sun to warm the surface. Deduct if the student attributes the difference to Earth’s distance from the Sun. (pp. 69–71)

questions.stem: What is an analemma, and which two features of Earth’s motion give it its figure-eight shape?
questions.answer: A diagram showing the Sun’s position in the sky, viewed from a fixed place on Earth at the same mean solar time, as it varies over a year. The shape comes from Earth’s axial tilt and its orbital eccentricity.
questions.rubric: 1.5 pts for the definition — a plot of the Sun’s position from one fixed location at the same clock time across a full year. 1.5 pts for both causes: axial tilt (obliquity), which produces the north–south component, and the eccentricity of Earth’s orbit, which produces the east–west component (the equation of time). Full credit if the student notes that with a circular orbit and no tilt the analemma would be a single dot. (pp. 72–74)
